Community colleges typically offer classes like fundamentals of nursing, microbiology, anatomy, and physiology to support nursing course work. Once you transition into your nursing program, the curriculum will typically include classes such as nutrition, pharmacology, medical-surgical nursing, pediatrics, geriatrics, and mental health nursing.

Second, nursing schools and community colleges tend to have smaller class sizes, which allows for more one-on-one instruction by the nursing instructors. Third, nursing school is where you will begin your study of clinical nursing scenarios and develop your muscle memory for tasks like starting intravenous lines and collecting medical history information.

During your nursing program, you will also schedule clinical rotations at hospitals, clinics, long-term care facilities or other healthcare settings. Clinical rotations provide hands-on experience with real patients while you are guided by an experienced nurse. You will begin to apply your school-based study to real people with complex healthcare needs. 

After completing your associate degree in nursing, you will then take an exam called NCLEX-RN to receive your nursing license. After receiving your license, you can choose to work as a newly-licensed nurse for a few years or attend a bachelors degree in nursing program (BSN) which will prepare you to be an advanced practice registered nurse or work in higher medical settings, such as a hospital environment, or other facilities. 

Overall, study will take place within a nursing program supplemented by clinical rotation to get the most value from your education and become a nurse.

prompt: Explain how compound interest works.
answer: Compound interest is calculated on both the initial amount invested or loaned, as well as the interest accrued in previous periods. This means that interest is earned on both the principal and previously accrued interest. Compound interest has two key variables: the principal amount and the compounding frequency. The more frequent the compounding (e.g., daily instead of monthly), the greater the compound interest accrued over time. As a general rule, compound interest works in your favor when saving and investing money, and it works against you when paying off debt.

prompt: Explain how compound interest works.
answer:
Compound interest is the process of earning interest on interest, that has already been earned. That is, when you save or invest money, interest is paid on your original deposit, but also on the accumulated interest from previous periods. Compound interest therefore accelerates the growth of your money over time. 

To illustrate, let's assume you deposit $10,000 at an annual interest rate of 5% in an account that compounds interest annually. After the first year you would have earned $500 in interest, for a total balance of $10,500. In the second year you would earn 5% on both the original $10,000 plus the additional $500, so your new balance would be $11,025, with the $525 representing interest earned on interest. As this process continues your balance grows at an increasing rate. 

It is worth noting that the power of compound interest is heavily dependent on how often the interest is compounded. For example, if the 5% interest rate paid above was compounded monthly it would earn interest 12 times a year, rather than once. This would lead to even faster growth, as interest would be earned even on the interest from the previous month. Likewise, if the interest was only compounded yearly, the interest rate would only be earned once a year, leading to less growth than if it was compounded monthly. 

Compound interest is a powerful concept that can be used to grow wealth over time. It is often referred to as the eighth wonder of the world because of how much it can grow your money. It is especially useful when saving or investing for long term goals like retirement, and can be compounded monthly, quarterly, semi-monthly, or even daily. It is very important to understand how your money is being compounded when saving and investing, as it can have a major impact on the amount of growth you will see.

prompt: Explain how compound interest works.
answer: Compound interest refers to earning interest on previously earned interest, in addition to the original principal. This is in contrast to simple interest, which is interest earned only on the original principal. The formula for compound interest is A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where A is the final amount, P is the principal amount, r is the annual interest rate, n is the number of times that interest is compounded per year, and t is the number of years the money is invested for. For example, if you invest $1,000 at an annual interest rate of 5%, compounded monthly, for 5 years, the formula would be A = 1,000(1 + 0.05/12)^(12*5) = $1,283.36. This means that you would earn $283.36 in interest over the course of 5 years, in addition to your original $1,000 principal. This is because you are earning interest on the interest that was accumulated each month. The more frequently interest is compounded, the more you will earn due to compound interest. For example, if the interest was compounded daily, the formula would be A = 1,000(1 + 0.05/365)^(365*5) = $1,284.01. This is because you are earning interest on the interest that was accumulated each day. Overall, compound interest is a powerful tool for growth and can help you save money over time.

In the spring and fall, neither hemisphere is tilted toward the sun, leading to temperatures and daylight hours that fall between those of summer and winter.
